subject: physics
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: What is the SI unit of force?
questions.explain: Force is measured in newtons (N) on the Edexcel International GCSE specification.

questions.q: Which of these is the correct unit for momentum?
questions.explain: Momentum is mass × velocity, so its unit is kilogram metre per second (kg m/s).

questions.q: What is the correct unit for acceleration?
questions.explain: Acceleration is the change in velocity per second, giving units of metres per second squared (m/s²).

questions.q: Which quantity is measured in newtons?
questions.explain: Weight is a force, so it is measured in newtons, whereas mass is measured in kilograms.

questions.q: Which equation correctly gives average speed?
questions.explain: Average speed is calculated by dividing the distance travelled by the time taken.

questions.q: Which equation gives acceleration?
questions.explain: Acceleration is the change in velocity (final minus initial) divided by the time taken.

questions.q: What does the gradient of a distance-time graph represent?
questions.explain: The steeper the line on a distance-time graph, the greater the speed, so the gradient equals speed.

questions.q: What does the area under a velocity-time graph represent?
questions.explain: The area beneath a velocity-time graph gives the distance travelled by the object.

questions.q: A horizontal (flat) line on a distance-time graph shows that the object is:
questions.explain: A flat line means the distance is not changing, so the object is stationary.

questions.q: A car travels 100 m in 5 s. What is its average speed?
questions.explain: Speed = distance ÷ time = 100 ÷ 5 = 20 m/s.

questions.q: A car starts from rest and accelerates at 2 m/s² over a distance of 25 m. Using v² = u² + 2as, what is its final velocity?
Which equation links resultant force, mass and acceleration?
questions.explain: The resultant force equals mass multiplied by acceleration (Newton's second law).

questions.q: A resultant force acts on a 4 kg object, giving it an acceleration of 3 m/s². What is the size of the force?
When the resultant force on a moving object is zero, the object will:
questions.explain: With no resultant force, an object keeps moving at a steady speed in a straight line.

questions.q: Hooke's law for a spring is best written as:
questions.explain: The force is proportional to the extension, where k is the spring constant (F = kx).

questions.q: Beyond its limit of proportionality, a stretched spring:
questions.explain: Past the limit of proportionality, extension is no longer proportional to force, so Hooke's law fails.

questions.q: Which equation gives the momentum of a moving object?
questions.explain: Momentum equals mass multiplied by velocity (p = mv).

questions.q: A 2 kg trolley moves at 5 m/s. What is its momentum?
questions.explain: Momentum = mass × velocity = 2 × 5 = 10 kg m/s.

questions.q: The total stopping distance of a car is made up of:
questions.explain: Stopping distance is the sum of the thinking distance and the braking distance.

questions.q: The moment of a force about a pivot is calculated as:
options: Force × perpendicular distance from the pivot
questions.explain: A moment equals the force multiplied by the perpendicular distance from the line of action to the pivot.

specSource: Pearson Edexcel International GCSE Physics (4PH1) specification; Forces & Motion
